focus: Anchor in THIS card: 'Ciò premesso' = 'that having been stated' – a past participle standing alone as a whole clause in formal Italian; drop the borrowed Finito-il-lavoro example.
'Fermo restando' is literally 'remaining firm' – a frozen legal/formal opener meaning 'without prejudice to'; quote this card, not Detto questo.
'L'aver studiato' = 'the having studied' – Italian puts l' before an infinitive to turn it into a noun where English uses -ing; give a hook, cut 'compound nominalized infinitive'.
'Per quanto' = 'however much' and always drags the verb into the subjunctive (possa sembrare); say the rule, not just the label.
'Bisogna che' + subjunctive (io studi) – and bisogna is subjectless: 'io bisogno' doesn't exist; quote bisogna itself, not just 'che'.
'Mica male' = 'not bad at all' – colloquial mica strengthens or, as here, entirely replaces non; quote the card and add the gloss.
'Senza che' takes the subjunctive (se ne accorgesse) – and Italian stacks it with nessuno where English says 'anyone'; lead with that trap.
'Per la quale' is the formal written cousin of 'per cui' – la quale agrees with l'azienda; make the register contrast the point, drop the 'combines' framing.
'Avendo finito' = 'having finished' – avendo + participle marks an action completed before the main verb; plain words, no 'gerundio passato' label.
'Purché' = 'provided that' and always takes the subjunctive (venga fatta); give the gloss first, cut 'formal conditional clause with passive'.
'Lungi dall'essere' = 'far from being' – lungi is an archaic 'far' that survives only in this formal formula; add the literal gloss.
'Ce la metto tutta' – ce and la are frozen parts of mettercela tutta ('put it all there'); la points at nothing, and that's the trap; don't just re-translate.
'Ho fatto riparare' = 'I made repair' – fare + infinitive means someone else did it for you, Italian's standard way to 'get X done'.
'Non ce la faccio più' – farcela = to manage/cope; ce and la are fixed inside the verb, and più supplies the 'anymore'.
'Se la prende' – prendersela = to get upset/take it personally; add con for the target: se la prende con me.
Re-anchor on THIS card: 'andando avanti così' – the bare gerund covers English 'if/by going on like this' with no word for if or by; drop the Rispose-ridendo example.
'Foss'anche' = 'were it even' – literary se-less inversion, foss' is elided fosse; gloss it, drop 'emphatic concessive'.
'Non fosse stato per te' = 'had it not been for you' – Italian drops se and inverts exactly like formal English; make that parallel the hook.
'Sia come sia' is literally 'be it as it be' – frozen subjunctive, the cousin of English 'be that as it may'.
Reported future becomes PAST conditional: arriverò → 'sarebbe arrivato', never arriverebbe; also fix the missing accent (tip has 'Arrivero').
'A prescindere da' = 'regardless of' – and the open-ended ciò che pushes the verb to subjunctive (abbiano deciso); gloss first.
'Avesse almeno avuto' with no se = 'if only he had' – a bare pluperfect subjunctive voicing regret; plain words, drop 'desiderative'.
'Pur essendo stanco' = 'despite being tired' – pur + gerund squeezes a whole although-clause into two words.
